behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest. <hi type="super">36</hi> And he that reapeth receiveth wages, and gathereth fruit unto life eternal: that both he that soweth and he that reapeth may rejoice together. <hi type="super">37</hi> And herein is that saying true, One soweth, and another reapeth. <hi type="super">38</hi> I sent you to reap that whereon ye bestowed no labour: other men laboured, and ye are entered into their labours. <hi type="super">39</hi> And many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman, which testified, He told me all that ever I did. <hi type="super">40</hi> So when the Samaritans were come unto him, they besought him that he would tarry with them: and he abode there two days. <hi type="super">41</hi> And many more believed because of his own word; <hi type="super">42</hi> And said unto the woman, Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard <hi type="italic">him</hi> ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world. <div eID="gen26919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26920" type="x-p"/> We have here the remainder of the story of what happened when Christ was in Samaria, after the long conference he had with the woman. <div eID="gen26920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26921" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">interruption given to this discourse</hi> by the disciples' coming. It is probable that much more was said than is recorded; but just when the discourse was brought to a head, when Christ had made himself known to her as the true Messiah, <hi type="italic">then came the disciples.</hi> The <hi type="italic">daughters of Jerusalem</hi> shall not <hi type="italic">stir up nor awake my love till he please.</hi> 1. They wondered at Christ's converse with this woman, marvelled that he talked thus earnestly (as perhaps they observed at a distance) with a woman, a strange woman alone (he used to be more <hi type="italic">reserved</hi>), especially with a Samaritan woman, that was not of the lost sheep of the house of Israel; they thought their Master should be as shy of the Samaritans as the other Jews were, at least that he should not preach the gospel to them. They wondered he should condescend to talk with such a poor contemptible woman, forgetting what despicable men they themselves were when Christ first called them into fellowship with himself. 2. Yet they acquiesced in it; they knew it was for some good reason, and some good end, of which he was not bound to give them an account, and therefore none of them asked, <hi type="italic">What seekest thou?</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Why talkest thou with her?</hi> Thus, when particular difficulties occur in the word and providence of God, it is good to satisfy ourselves with this in general, that all is well which Jesus Christ saith and doeth. Perhaps there was something <hi type="italic">amiss</hi> in their <hi type="italic">marveling</hi> that <hi type="italic">Christ talked with the woman:</hi> it was something like the Pharisees being offended at his eating with publicans and sinners. But, whatever they <hi type="italic">thought,</hi> they said <hi type="italic">nothing. If thou hast thought evil</hi> at any time, <hi type="italic">lay thy hand upon thy mouth,</hi> to keep that evil thought from turning into an evil word, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.32">Prov. xxx. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.3">Ps. xxxix. 1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen26921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26922" type="x-p"/> The notice which the woman gave to her neighbours of the extraordinary person she had happily met with, <reference osisRef="John.4.28-John.4.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen26922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26923" type="x-p"/> 1. How she <hi type="italic">forgot her errand to the well,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.28">v. 28</reference>. Therefore, because the disciples were come, and broke up the discourse, and perhaps she observed they were not pleased with it, she <hi type="italic">went her way.</hi> She withdrew, in civility to Christ, that he might have leisure to <hi type="italic">eat his dinner.</hi> She delighted in his discourse, but would not be <hi type="italic">rude;</hi> every thing is beautiful in its season. She supposed that Jesus, when he had dined, would go forward in his journey, and therefore hastened to tell her neighbours, that they might come quickly. <hi type="italic">Yet a little while is the light with you.</hi> See how she improved time; when one good work was done, she applied herself to another. When opportunities of <hi type="italic">getting good</hi> cease, or are interrupted, we should seek opportunities of <hi type="italic">doing good;</hi> when we have done <hi type="italic">hearing</hi> the word, then is a time to be <hi type="italic">speaking</hi> of it. Notice is taken of her <hi type="italic">leaving her water-pot</hi> or <hi type="italic">pail.</hi> (1.) She left it in kindness to Christ, that he might have water to drink; he turned water into wine for others, but not for himself. Compare this with Rebecca's civility to Abraham's servant (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.18">Gen. xxiv. 18</reference>), and see that promise, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.42">Matt. x. 42</reference>. (2.) She left it that she might make the more haste into the city, to carry thither these good tidings. Those whose business it is to publish the name of Christ must not encumber or entangle themselves with any thing that will retard or hinder them therein. When the disciples are to be made fishers of men they must <hi type="italic">forsake all.</hi> (3.) She left her water-pot, as one <hi type="italic">careless of it,</hi> being wholly taken up with better things. Note, Those who are brought to the knowledge of Christ will show it by a holy contempt of this world and the things of it. And those who are <hi type="italic">newly</hi> acquainted with the things of God must be <hi type="italic">excused,</hi> if at first they be so taken up with the new world into which they are brought that the things of this world seem to be for a time wholly neglected. Mr. Hildersham, in one of his sermons on this verse, from this instance largely justifies those who leave their worldly business on week-days to go to hear sermons. <div eID="gen26923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26924" type="x-p"/> 2. How she <hi type="italic">minded her errand to the town,</hi> for her heart was upon it. She <hi type="italic">went into the city,</hi> and said to <hi type="italic">the men,</hi> probably the aldermen, the men in authority, whom, it may be, she found met together upon some public business; or to <hi type="italic">the men,</hi> that is, to every man she met in the streets; she proclaimed it in the chief places of concourse: <hi type="italic">Come, see a man who told me all things that ever I did. Is not this the Christ?</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26925" type="x-p"/> (1.) How <hi type="italic">solicitous</hi> she was to <hi type="italic">have her friends and neighbours</hi> acquainted with Christ. When she had found that treasure, she <hi type="italic">called together her friends and neighbours</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Luke.15.9">Luke xv. 9</reference>), not only to <hi type="italic">rejoice with her,</hi> but to share with her, knowing there was enough to enrich herself and all that would partake with her. Note, They that have been themselves with Jesus, and have found comfort in him, should do all they can to bring others to him. Has he done us the honour to make himself known to us? Let us do him the honour to make him known to others; nor can we do ourselves a greater honour. This woman becomes an apostle. <hi type="italic">Quæ scortum fuerat egressa, regreditur magistra evangelica—She who went forth a specimen of impurity returns a teacher of evangelical truth,</hi> saith <hi type="italic">Aretius.</hi> Christ had told her to <hi type="italic">call her husband,</hi> which she thought was warrant enough to <hi type="italic">call every body.</hi> She went into <hi type="italic">the city,</hi> the city where she dwelt, among her kinsfolks and acquaintance. Though every man is my neighbour that I have opportunity of doing good to, yet I have most <hi type="italic">opportunity,</hi> and therefore lie under the greatest <hi type="italic">obligations,</hi> to do good to those that live near me. <hi type="italic">Where the tree falls,</hi> there let it be made useful. <div eID="gen26925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26926" type="x-p"/> (2.) How fair and ingenuous she was in the notice she gave them concerning this stranger she had met with. [1.] She <hi type="italic">tells them</hi> plainly what induced her to admire him: <hi type="italic">He has told me all things that ever I did.</hi> No more is recorded than what he told her of her husbands; but it is not improbable that he had told her of more of her faults. Or, his telling her that which she knew he could not by any ordinary means come to the knowledge of convinced her that he could have told her all that she ever did. If he has a <hi type="italic">divine</hi> knowledge, it must be omniscience. He told her that which none knew but God and her own conscience. Two things affected her:—<hi type="italic">First, the extent of his knowledge.</hi> We ourselves cannot tell <hi type="italic">all things that ever we did</hi> (many things pass <hi type="italic">unheeded,</hi> and more pass away and are forgotten); but Jesus Christ knows all the thoughts, words, and actions, of all the children of men; see <reference osisRef="Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 13</reference>. He hath said, <hi type="italic">I know thy works. Secondly, The power of his word.</hi> This made a great impression upon her, that he told her her <hi type="italic">secret sins</hi> with such an unaccountable power and energy that, being told of one, she is <hi type="italic">convinced of all, and judged of all.</hi> She does not say, "Come, see a man that has told me strange things concerning religious worship, and the laws of it, that has decided the controversy between this mountain and Jerusalem, a man that calls himself the <hi type="italic">Messias;</hi>" but, "<hi type="italic">Come see a man</hi> that has told me of my sins." She fastens upon that part of Christ's discourse which one would think she would have been most shy of repeating; but experimental proofs of the power of Christ's word and Spirit are of all others the most cogent and convincing; and that <hi type="italic">knowledge of Christ</hi> into which we are led by the conviction of sin and humiliation is most likely to be <hi type="italic">sound</hi> and <hi type="italic">saving.</hi> [2.] She <hi type="italic">invites them</hi> to <hi type="italic">come and see</hi> him of whom she had conceived so high an opinion. Not barely, "Come and look upon him" (she does not invite them to him as a <hi type="italic">show</hi>), but, "Come and converse with him; come and <hi type="italic">hear his wisdom,</hi> as I have done, and you will be of my mind." She would not undertake to manage the arguments which had convinced her, in such a manner as to convince others; all that see the evidence of truth themselves are not able to make others see it; but, "Come, and talk with him, and you will find such a power in his word as far exceeds all other evidence." Note, Those who can do little else towards the conviction and conversion of others may and should bring them to those means of grace which they themselves have found effectual. Jesus was now at the town's end. "Now come see him." When opportunities of getting the knowledge of God are brought to our doors we are inexcusable if we neglect them; shall we not go over the threshold to see him whose day prophets and kings desired to see? [3.] She resolves to <hi type="italic">appeal to themselves,</hi> and their own sentiments upon the trial. <hi type="italic">Is not this the Christ?</hi> She does not peremptorily say, "He is the Messiah," how clear soever she was in her own mind, and yet she very prudently mentions the Messiah, of whom otherwise they would not have thought, and then refers it to themselves; she will not impose her faith upon them, but only propose it to them. By such fair but forcible appeals as these men's judgments and consciences are sometimes taken hold of ere they are aware. <div eID="gen26926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26927" type="x-p"/> (3.) What success she had in this invitation: <hi type="italic">They went out of the city, and came to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.30">v. 30</reference>. Though it might seem very improbable that a woman of so <hi type="italic">small</hi> a figure, and so <hi type="italic">ill</hi> a character, should have the honour of the first discovery of the Messiah among the Samaritans, yet it pleased God to incline their hearts to take notice of her report, and not to slight it as an idle tale. Time was when lepers were the first that brought tidings to Samaria of a great deliverance, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.3">2 Kings vii. 3</reference>, &c. They <hi type="italic">came unto him;</hi> did not send for him into the city to them, but in token of their respect to him, and the earnestness of their desire to see him, they <hi type="italic">went out to him.</hi> Those that would know Christ must meet him where he records his name. <div eID="gen26927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26928" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's discourse with his disciples while the woman was absent, <reference osisRef="John.4.31-John.4.38">v. 31-38</reference>. See how industrious our Lord Jesus was to <hi type="italic">redeem time,</hi> to husband every minute of it, and to <hi type="italic">fill up</hi> the vacancies of it. When the disciples were gone into the town, his discourse with the woman was <hi type="italic">edifying,</hi> and suited to her case; when she was gone into the town, his discourse with them was no less edifying, and suited to their case; it were well if we could <hi type="italic">thus</hi> gather up the fragments of time, that none of it may be lost. Two things are observable in this discourse:— <div eID="gen26928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26929" type="x-p"/> 1. How Christ <hi type="italic">expresses the delight</hi> which he himself had in his work. His work was to <hi type="italic">seek and save</hi> that which was lost, to go about doing good. Now with this work we here find him wholly taken up. For, <div eID="gen26929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26930" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">He neglected his meat and drink for his work.</hi> When he sat down upon the well, he was <hi type="italic">weary,</hi> and needed refreshment; but this opportunity of saving souls made him forget his weariness and hunger. And he minded <hi type="italic">his food</hi> so little that, [1.] His disciples were forced to invite him to it: <hi type="italic">They prayed him,</hi> they pressed him, saying, <hi type="italic">Master, eat.</hi> It was an instance of their <hi type="italic">love to him</hi> that they invited him, lest he should be faint and sick for want of some support; but it was a greater instance of his <hi type="italic">love to souls</hi> that he needed invitation. Let us learn hence a holy indifference even to the needful supports of life, in comparison with spiritual things. [2.] He minded it so little that they suspected he had had meat brought him in their absence (<reference osisRef="John.4.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Has any man brought him aught to eat?</hi> He had so little appetite for his dinner that they were ready to think he had dined already. Those that make religion their business will, when any of its affairs are to be attended, prefer them before their food; as Abraham's servant, that would not eat till he had told his errand (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.33">Gen. xxiv. 33</reference>), and Samuel, that would not sit down till David was anointed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.11">1 Sam. xvi. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen26930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26931" type="x-p"/> (2.) He <hi type="italic">made his work his meat and drink.</hi> The work he <hi type="italic">had to do</hi> among the Samaritans, the prospect he now had of doing good to many, this was <hi type="italic">meat and drink</hi> to him; it was the greatest pleasure and satisfaction imaginable. Never did a hungry man, or an epicure, expect a plentiful feast with so much desire, nor feed upon its dainties with so much delight, as our Lord Jesus expected and improved an opportunity of doing good to souls. Concerning this he saith, [1.] That it was such <hi type="italic">meat</hi> as the disciples <hi type="italic">knew not of.</hi> They did not imagine that he had any design or prospect of planting his gospel among the Samaritans; this was a piece of usefulness they never thought of. Note, Christ by his gospel and Spirit does more good to the souls of men than his own disciples <hi type="italic">know of</hi> or <hi type="italic">expect.</hi> This may be said of good Christians too, who live by faith, that they have meat to eat which others know not of, joy with which a stranger does not intermeddle. Now this word made them ask, <hi type="italic">Has any man brought him aught to eat?</hi> so apt were even his own disciples to understand him after a corporal and carnal manner when he used similitudes. [2.] That the reason why his work was his meat and drink was because it was his Father's work, his Father's will: <hi type="italic">My meat is to do the will of him that sent me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.34">v. 34</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The salvation of sinners is the <hi type="italic">will of God,</hi> and the instruction of them in order thereunto is <hi type="italic">his work.</hi> See <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1 Tim. ii. 4</reference>. There is a chosen remnant whose salvation is in a particular manner his will. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ was <hi type="italic">sent into the world</hi> on this errand, to bring people to God, to know him and to be happy in him. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He made this work his business and delight. When his body needed food, his mind was so taken up with this that he forgot both hunger and thirst, both meat and drink. Nothing could be more grateful to him than doing good; when he was invited <hi type="italic">to meat</hi> he went, that he might <hi type="italic">do good,</hi> for that was his meat always. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He was not only ready upon all occasions to go to his work, but he was <hi type="italic">earnest</hi> and in care to go <hi type="italic">through</hi> it, and to <hi type="italic">finish his work</hi> in all the parts of it. He resolved never to quit it, nor lay it down, till he could say, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> Many have zeal to carry them <hi type="italic">out</hi> at first, but not zeal to carry them <hi type="italic">on</hi> to the last; but our Lord Jesus was intent upon <hi type="italic">finishing his work.</hi> Our Master has herein left us an example, that we may learn to do the will of God as he did; 1. With diligence and close application, as those that make a business of it. 2. With delight and pleasure in it, as in our element. 3. With constancy and perseverance; not only minding to <hi type="italic">do,</hi> but aiming to <hi type="italic">finish,</hi> our work. <div eID="gen26931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26932" type="x-p"/> 2. See here how Christ, having expressed his delight in <hi type="italic">his</hi> work, excites his disciples to diligence in <hi type="italic">their</hi> work; they were workers <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> and therefore should be workers <hi type="italic">like him,</hi> and make their work their <hi type="italic">meat,</hi> as he did. The work they had to do was to <hi type="italic">preach the gospel,</hi> and to set up the kingdom of the Messiah. Now this work he here compares to <hi type="italic">harvest work,</hi> the gathering in of the fruits of the earth; and this similitude he prosecutes throughout the discourse, <reference osisRef="John.4.35-John.4.38">v. 35-38</reference>. Note, gospel time is harvest time, and gospel work harvest work. The harvest is before <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> and expected; so was the gospel. Harvest time is <hi type="italic">busy</hi> time; all hands must be then at work: every one must work for <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> that he may reap of the graces and comforts of the gospel: ministers must work <hi type="italic">for God,</hi> to gather in souls to him. Harvest time is <hi type="italic">opportunity,</hi> a short and limited time, which will not last always; and harvest work is work that must be done <hi type="italic">then</hi> or not at all; so the time of the enjoyment of the gospel is a particular season, which must be improved for its proper purposes; for, once past, it cannot be recalled. The disciples were to gather in a harvest of souls for Christ. Now he here suggests three things to them to quicken them to diligence:— <div eID="gen26932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26933" type="x-p"/> (1.) That it was <hi type="italic">necessary work,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">occasion</hi> for it very urgent and pressing (<reference osisRef="John.4.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">You say, It is four months to harvest;</hi> but I say, <hi type="italic">The fields are already white.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen26933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26934" type="x-p"/> [1.] A saying of Christ's disciples concerning the <hi type="italic">corn-harvest;</hi> there <hi type="italic">are yet four months, and then comes harvest,</hi> which may be taken either <hi type="italic">generally</hi>—"You say, for the encouragement of the sower at seed-time, that it will be but four months to the harvest." With us it is but about four months between the barley-sowing and the barley-harvest, probably it was so with them as to other grain; or, "Particularly, now at this time you reckon it will be four months to next harvest, according to the ordinary course of providence." The Jews' harvest began at the Passover, about Easter, much earlier in the year than ours, by which it appears that this journey of Christ from Judea to Galilee was in the winter, about the end of November, for he travelled <hi type="italic">all weathers</hi> to do good. God has not only promised us a harvest every year, but has appointed the <hi type="italic">weeks of harvest;</hi> so that we know <hi type="italic">when</hi> to expect it, and take our measures accordingly. <div eID="gen26934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26935" type="x-p"/> [2.] A saying of Christ's concerning the <hi type="italic">gospel harvest;</hi> his heart was as much upon the fruits of his gospel as the hearts of others were upon the fruits of the earth; and to this he would lead the thoughts of his disciples: <hi type="italic">Look, the fields are already white unto the harvest. First,</hi> Here in <hi type="italic">this</hi> place, where they <hi type="italic">now</hi> were, there was harvest work for <hi type="italic">him</hi> to do. They would have him to <hi type="italic">eat,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.31">v. 31</reference>. "Eat!" saith he, "I have other work to do, that is more needful; <hi type="italic">look</hi> what crowds of Samaritans are coming out of the town over the fields that are ready to receive the gospel;" probably there were many now in view. People's forwardness to hear the word is a great excitement to ministers' diligence and liveliness in preaching it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In <hi type="italic">other places,</hi> all the country over, there was harvest work enough for them all to do. "<hi type="italic">Consider the regions,</hi> think of the state of the country, and you will find there are multitudes as ready to receive the gospel as a field of corn that is fully ripe is ready to be reaped." The fields were now made <hi type="italic">white to the harvest,</hi> 1. By the <hi type="italic">decree of God</hi> revealed in the prophecies of the Old Testament. Now was the time when the gathering of the people should be to Christ ( <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>), when great accessions should be made to the church and the bounds of it should be enlarged, and therefore it was time for them to be busy. It is a great encouragement to us to engage in any work for God, if we understand by the signs of the times that this is the proper season for that work, for then it will prosper. 2. By the <hi type="italic">disposition of men.</hi> John Baptist had <hi type="italic">made ready a people prepared for the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Luke i. 17</reference>. Since he began to preach the kingdom of God <hi type="italic">every man pressed into it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Luke xvi. 16</reference>. This, therefore, was a time for the preachers of the gospel to apply themselves to their work with the utmost vigour, to <hi type="italic">thrust in their sickle,</hi> when the harvest was ripe, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Rev. xiv. 15</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">necessary</hi> to work now, pity that such a season should be let slip. If the corn that is <hi type="italic">ripe</hi> be not reaped, it will <hi type="italic">shed</hi> and be lost, and the fowls will pick it up. If souls that are under convictions, and have some good inclinations, be not helped now, their hopeful beginnings will come to nothing, and they will be a prey to pretenders. It was also <hi type="italic">easy</hi> to work now; when the people's hearts are <hi type="italic">prepared</hi> the work will be done <hi type="italic">suddenly,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.36">2 Chron. xxix. 36</reference>. It cannot but quicken ministers to take <hi type="italic">pains</hi> in preaching the word when they observe that people <hi type="italic">take pleasure</hi> in hearing it. <div eID="gen26935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26936" type="x-p"/> (2.) That it was <hi type="italic">profitable</hi> and <hi type="italic">advantageous</hi> work, which they themselves would be gainers by (<reference osisRef="John.4.36">v. 36</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He that reapeth receiveth wages,</hi> and so shall you." Christ has undertaken to pay those well whom he employs in his work; for he will never do as Jehoiakim did, <hi type="italic">who used his neighbour's service without wages</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jer. xxii. 13</reference>), or those who <hi type="italic">by fraud kept back the hire of those</hi> particularly <hi type="italic">who reaped their corn-fields,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jam. v. 4</reference>. Christ's reapers, though they cry <hi type="italic">to him</hi> day and night, shall never have cause to cry <hi type="italic">against him,</hi> nor to say they served a hard Master. He that reapeth, not only <hi type="italic">shall</hi> but <hi type="italic">does</hi> receive wages. There is a present reward in the service of Christ, and his work is <hi type="italic">its own wages.</hi> [1.] Christ's reapers have <hi type="italic">fruit: He gathereth fruit unto life eternal;</hi> that is, he shall both save himself and those that hear him, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.16">1 Tim. iv. 16</reference>. If the faithful reaper save his own soul, that is fruit abounding to his account, it is fruit gathered to <hi type="italic">life eternal;</hi> and if, over and above this, he be instrumental to save the souls of others too, there is <hi type="italic">fruit gathered.</hi> Souls gathered to Christ are fruit, good fruit, the fruit that Christ seeks for (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.13">Rom. i. 13</reference>); it is gathered for Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.8.11-Song.8.12">Cant. viii. 11, 12</reference>); it is gathered to <hi type="italic">life eternal.</hi> This is the comfort of faithful ministers, that their work has a tendency to the eternal salvation of precious souls. [2.] They have <hi type="italic">joy: That he that sows and they that reap may rejoice together.</hi> The minister who is the happy instrument of beginning a good work is <hi type="italic">he that sows,</hi> as John Baptist; he that is employed to carry it on and perfect it is <hi type="italic">he that reaps:</hi> and both shall rejoice together. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Though God is to have all the glory of the success of the gospel, yet faithful ministers may themselves take the comfort of it. The reapers share in the <hi type="italic">joy of harvest,</hi> though the profits belong to the master, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1 Thess. ii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those ministers who are variously gifted and employed should be so far from envying one another that they should rather mutually rejoice in each other's success and usefulness. Though all Christ's ministers are not alike <hi type="italic">serviceable,</hi> nor alike <hi type="italic">successful,</hi> yet, if they have obtained mercy of the Lord to be <hi type="italic">faithful,</hi> they shall all enter <hi type="italic">together into the joy of their Lord</hi> at last. <div eID="gen26936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26937" type="x-p"/> (3.) That it was <hi type="italic">easy work,</hi> and work that was half done to their hands by those that were gone before them: <hi type="italic">One soweth, and another reapeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.37-John.4.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. This sometimes denotes a grievous judgment upon him that sows, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.15">Mic. vi. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">Deut. xxviii. 30</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt sow, and another shall reap;</hi> as <reference osisRef="Deut.6.11">Deut. vi. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not.</hi> So here. Moses, and the prophets, and John Baptist, had <hi type="italic">paved</hi> the way to the gospel, had sown the good seed which the New-Testament ministers did in effect but gather the fruit of. <hi type="italic">I send you to reap that whereon you bestowed,</hi> in comparison, no <hi type="italic">labour.</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3-Isa.40.5">Isa. xl. 3-5</reference>. [1.] This intimates <hi type="italic">two things</hi> concerning the Old-Testament ministry:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That it was very much <hi type="italic">short</hi> of the New-Testament ministry. Moses and the <hi type="italic">prophets</hi> sowed, but they could not be said to <hi type="italic">reap,</hi> so little did they see of the fruit of their labours. Their writings have done much more good since they left us than ever their preaching did. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it was very <hi type="italic">serviceable</hi> to the New-Testament ministry, and made way for it. The writings of the prophets, which were read in the synagogues every sabbath day, raised people's expectations of the Messiah, and so prepared them to bid him welcome. Had it not been for the seed sown by the prophets, this Samaritan woman could not have said, <hi type="italic">We know that Messias cometh.</hi> The writings of the Old Testament are in some respects more useful to us than they could be to those to whom they were first written, because better understood by the accomplishment of them. See <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1 Pet. i. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">Heb. iv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25-Rom.16.26">Rom. xvi. 25, 26</reference>. [2.] This also intimates <hi type="italic">two things</hi> concerning the ministry of the <hi type="italic">apostles of Christ. First,</hi> That it was a <hi type="italic">fruitful</hi> ministry: they were reapers that gathered in a great harvest of souls to Jesus Christ, and did more in seven years towards the setting up of the kingdom of God among men than the prophets of the Old Testament had done in twice so many ages. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it was much <hi type="italic">facilitated,</hi> especially among the Jews, to whom they were first sent, by the writings of the prophets. The prophets <hi type="italic">sowed in tears,</hi> crying out, <hi type="italic">We have laboured in vain;</hi> the apostles <hi type="italic">reaped in joy,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God, who always causeth us to triumph.</hi> Note, From the labours of ministers that are dead and gone much good fruit may be reaped by the people that <hi type="italic">survive</hi> them and the ministers that <hi type="italic">succeed</hi> them. John Baptist, and those that assisted him, had <hi type="italic">laboured,</hi> and the disciples of Christ entered into their labours, built upon their foundation, and reaped the fruit of what they sowed. See what reason we have to bless God for those that are <hi type="italic">gone before us,</hi> for their preaching and their writing, for what they <hi type="italic">did</hi> and <hi type="italic">suffered</hi> in their day, for we are <hi type="italic">entered into their labours;</hi> their studies and services have made our work the easier. And when the ancient and modern labourers, those that came into the vineyard at the third hour and those that came in at the eleventh, meet in the day of account, they will be so far from envying one another the honour of their respective services that both <hi type="italic">they that sowed</hi> and they that <hi type="italic">reaped</hi> shall rejoice together; and the great Lord of thee harvest shall have the glory of all. <div eID="gen26937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26938" type="x-p"/> IV. The <hi type="italic">good effect</hi> which this visit Christ made to the Samaritans (<hi type="italic">en passant</hi>) had upon them, and the fruit which was now presently gathered among them, <reference osisRef="John.4.39-John.4.42">v. 39-42</reference>. See what impressions were made on them, <div eID="gen26938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26939" type="x-p"/> 1. By the <hi type="italic">woman's testimony</hi> concerning <hi type="italic">Christ;</hi> though a single testimony, and of one of no good report, and the testimony no more than this, <hi type="italic">He told me all that ever I did,</hi> yet it had a good influence upon many. One would have thought that his telling the woman of her secret sins would have made them afraid of coming to him, lest he should tell them also of their faults; but they will venture that rather than not be acquainted with one who they had reason to think was a prophet. And <hi type="italic">two things</hi> they were brought to:— <div eID="gen26939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26940" type="x-p"/> (1.) To <hi type="italic">credit</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">word</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman.</hi> So far they <hi type="italic">believed on him</hi> that they took him for a <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> and were desirous to know the mind of God from him; this is favourably interpreted as believing on him. Now observe, [1.] Who they were that believed: <hi type="italic">Many of the Samaritans,</hi> who were not of the house of Israel. Their faith was not only an <hi type="italic">aggravation</hi> of the <hi type="italic">unbelief</hi> of the Jews, from whom better might have been expected, but an <hi type="italic">earnest</hi> of the <hi type="italic">faith</hi> of the Gentiles, who would welcome that which the Jews rejected. [2.] Upon what inducement they believed: <hi type="italic">For the saying of the woman.</hi> See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How God is sometimes pleased to use very weak and unlikely instruments for the beginning and carrying on of a good work. A little maid directed a great prince to Elisha, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.2">2 Kings v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How great a matter a little fire kindles. Our Saviour, by instructing one poor woman, spread instruction to a whole town. Let not ministers be either <hi type="italic">careless</hi> in their preaching, or <hi type="italic">discouraged</hi> in it, because their hearers are <hi type="italic">few</hi> and <hi type="italic">mean;</hi> for, by doing good to <hi type="italic">them,</hi> good may be conveyed to <hi type="italic">more,</hi> and those that are more considerable. If they <hi type="italic">teach every man his neighbour,</hi> and <hi type="italic">every man his brother,</hi> a great number may learn at <hi type="italic">second hand.</hi> Philip preached the gospel to a single gentleman in his chariot upon the road, and he not only received it himself, but carried it into his country, and propagated it there. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> See how good it is to speak <hi type="italic">experimentally</hi> of Christ and the things of God. This woman could say little of Christ, but what she did say she spoke feelingly: <hi type="italic">He told me all that ever I did.</hi> Those are most likely to do good that can tell what God has done <hi type="italic">for their souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen26940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26941" type="x-p"/> (2.) They were brought to <hi type="italic">court his stay</hi> among them (<reference osisRef="John.4.40">v. 40</reference>): When they were come to him <hi type="italic">they besought him that he would tarry with them.</hi> Upon the woman's report, they believed him to be a prophet, and <hi type="italic">came to him;</hi> and, when they <hi type="italic">saw</hi> him, the meanness of his appearance and the manifest poverty of his outward condition did not lessen their esteem of him and expectations from him, but still they respected him as a prophet. Note, There is hope of those who are got over the vulgar prejudices that men have against <hi type="italic">true worth</hi> in a <hi type="italic">low estate.</hi> Blessed are they that are not offended in Christ at the <hi type="italic">first sight.</hi> So far were they from being offended in him that they begged he would tarry with them; [1.] That they might <hi type="italic">testify their respect</hi> to him, and treat him with the honour and kindness due to his character. God's prophets and ministers are welcome guests to all those who sincerely embrace the gospel; as to Lydia, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.15">Acts xvi. 15</reference>. [2.] That they might receive instruction from him. Those that are taught of God are truly desirous to learn more, and to be better acquainted with Christ. Many would have flocked to one that would tell them <hi type="italic">their fortune,</hi> but these flocked to one that would tell them <hi type="italic">their faults,</hi> tell them of their sin and duty. The historian seems to lay an emphasis upon their being Samaritans; as <reference osisRef="Luke.10.33">Luke x. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.17.16">xvii. 16</reference>. The Samaritans had not that reputation for religion which the Jews had; yet the Jews, who saw Christ's miracles, drove him from them: while the Samaritans, who saw not his miracles, nor shared in his favours, invited him to them. The <hi type="italic">proof</hi> of the gospel's success is not always according to the <hi type="italic">probability,</hi> nor what is <hi type="italic">experienced</hi> according to what is <hi type="italic">expected</hi> either way. The Samaritans were taught by the custom of their country to be shy of conversation with the Jews. There were Samaritans that refused to let Christ go through their town (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.53">Luke ix. 53</reference>), but these begged him to tarry with them. Note, It adds much to the praise of our love to Christ and his word if it conquers the prejudices of education and custom, and sets light by the censures of men. Now we are told that Christ granted their request. <div eID="gen26941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26942" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He <hi type="italic">abode there.</hi> Though it was a city of the Samaritans nearly adjoining to their temple, yet, when he was <hi type="italic">invited,</hi> he <hi type="italic">tarried</hi> there; though he was upon a journey, and had further to go, yet, when he had an opportunity of doing good, he <hi type="italic">abode there.</hi> That is no real <hi type="italic">hindrance</hi> which will <hi type="italic">further</hi> our account. Yet he abode there but <hi type="italic">two days,</hi> because he had other places to visit and other work to do, and those <hi type="italic">two</hi> days were as many as came to the share of this city, out of the few days of our Saviour's sojourning upon earth. <div eID="gen26942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26943" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We are told what impressions were made upon them by Christ's own word, and his personal converse with them (<reference osisRef="John.4.41-John.4.42">v. 41, 42</reference>); what he <hi type="italic">said</hi> and <hi type="italic">did</hi> there is not related, whether he healed their sick or no; but it is intimated, in the effect, that he said and did that which convinced them that he was the Christ; and the labours of a minister are best told by the good fruit of them. Their hearing of <hi type="italic">him</hi> had a good effect, but <hi type="italic">now their eyes saw him;</hi> and the effect was, 1. That their number grew (<reference osisRef="John.4.41">v. 41</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many more believed:</hi> many that would not be persuaded to go out of the town to him were yet wrought upon, when he came among them, to believe in him. Note, It is comfortable to see the number of believers; and sometimes the zeal and forwardness of some may be a means to provoke many, and to stir them up to a holy emulation, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Rom. xi. 14</reference>. 2. That their faith grew. Those who had been wrought upon by the report of the woman now saw cause to say, <hi type="italic">Now we believe, not because of thy saying,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.42">v. 42</reference>. Here are three things in which their <hi type="italic">faith grew:</hi>—(1.) In the matter of it, or that which they did believe. Upon the testimony of the woman, they believed him to be <hi type="italic">a prophet,</hi> or some extraordinary messenger from heaven; but now that they have conversed with him they believe that he is <hi type="italic">the Christ,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Anointed One,</hi> the very same that was promised to the fathers and expected by them, and that, being the <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> he is the <hi type="italic">Saviour of the world;</hi> for the work to which he was anointed was to <hi type="italic">save his people from their sins.</hi> They believed him to be the Saviour not only of the Jews, but <hi type="italic">of the world,</hi> which they hoped would take them in, though Samaritans, for it was promised that he should be <hi type="italic">Salvation to the ends of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">Isa. xlix. 6</reference>. (2.) In the <hi type="italic">certainty</hi> of it; their faith now grew up to a full assurance: <hi type="italic">We know</hi> that this is indeed the <hi type="italic">Christ;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">alethos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">truly;</hi> not a pretended Christ, but a real one; not a <hi type="italic">typical</hi> Saviour, as many under the Old Testament, but <hi type="italic">truly</hi> one. Such an assurance as this of divine truths is what we should labour after; not only, We think it probable, and are willing to suppose that <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> may be the <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> but, We know that he is <hi type="italic">indeed the Christ.</hi> (3.) In the <hi type="italic">ground</hi> of it, which was a kind of spiritual sensation and experience: <hi type="italic">Now we believe, not because of thy saying, for we have heard him ourselves.</hi> They had before <hi type="italic">believed for her saying,</hi> and it was well, it was a good step; but now they find <hi type="italic">further</hi> and much <hi type="italic">firmer</hi> footing for their faith: "<hi type="italic">Now we believe</hi> because we have <hi type="italic">heard him ourselves,</hi> and have heard such excellent and divine truths, accompanied with such commanding power and evidence, that we are abundantly satisfied and assured that <hi type="italic">this is the Christ.</hi>" This is like what the queen of Sheba said of Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.6-1Kgs.10.7">1 Kings x. 6, 7</reference>): The <hi type="italic">one half was not told me.</hi> The Samaritans, who believed for the woman's saying, now gained further light; for <hi type="italic">to him that hath shall be given;</hi> he that is faithful in a little shall be trusted with more. In this instance we may see how <hi type="italic">faith comes by hearing.</hi> [1.] Faith comes <hi type="italic">to the birth</hi> by hearing the <hi type="italic">report of men.</hi> These Samaritans, for the sake of the woman's saying, believed so far as to <hi type="italic">come and see,</hi> to come and make trial. Thus the instructions of parents and preachers, and the testimony of the church and our experienced neighbours, <hi type="italic">recommend</hi> the doctrine of Christ <hi type="italic">to our acquaintance,</hi> and incline us to entertain it as highly probable. But, [2.] Faith <hi type="italic">comes to its growth,</hi> strength, and maturity, by hearing the testimony of Christ himself; and this goes further, and recommends his doctrine <hi type="italic">to our acceptance,</hi> and obliges us to believe it as undoubtedly certain. We were induced to look into the scriptures <hi type="italic">by the saying</hi> of those who told us that in them they had found eternal life; but when we ourselves have found it in them too, have experienced the enlightening, convincing, regenerating, sanctifying, comforting, power of the word, now we believe, <hi type="italic">not for their saying,</hi> but because we have searched them ourselves: and our faith <hi type="italic">stands not in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.5">1 Cor. ii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.9-1John.5.10">1 John v. 9, 10</reference>.
entries.fa516e368fbff04ca323440ec69bd5ee2640f515: <div eID="gen26943" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Nobleman's Son Restored.</title> <div sID="gen26944" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">43</hi> Now after two days he departed thence, and went into Galilee. <hi type="super">44</hi> For Jesus himself testified, that a prophet hath no honour in his own country. <hi type="super">45</hi> Then when he was come into Galilee, the Galilæans received him, having seen all the things that he did at Jerusalem at the feast: for they also went unto the feast. <hi type="super">46</hi> So Jesus came again into Cana of Galilee, where he made the water wine. And there was a certain nobleman, whose son was sick at Capernaum. <hi type="super">47</hi> When he heard that Jesus was come out of Judæa into Galilee, he went unto him, and besought him that he would come down, and heal his son: for he was at the point of death. <hi type="super">48</hi> Then said Jesus unto him, Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe. <hi type="super">49</hi> The nobleman saith unto him, Sir, come down ere my child die. <hi type="super">50</hi> Jesus saith unto him, Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way. <hi type="super">51</hi> And as he was now going down, his servants met him, and told <hi type="italic">him,</hi> saying, Thy son liveth. <hi type="super">52</hi> Then enquired he of them the hour when he began to amend. And they said unto him, Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him. <hi type="super">53</hi> So the father knew that <hi type="italic">it was</hi> at the same hour, in the which Jesus said unto him, Thy son liveth: and himself believed, and his whole house. <hi type="super">54</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> again the second miracle <hi type="italic">that</hi> Jesus did, when he was come out of Judæa into Galilee. <div eID="gen26944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26945" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen26945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26946" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's <hi type="italic">coming</hi> into Galilee, <reference osisRef="John.4.43">v. 43</reference>. Though he was as welcome among the Samaritans as he could be any where, and had better success, yet <hi type="italic">after two days</hi> he left them, not so much because they were Samaritans, and he would not confirm those in their prejudices against him who said, <hi type="italic">He is a Samaritan</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.48">ch. viii. 48</reference>), but because <hi type="italic">he must preach to other cities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.4.43">Luke iv. 43</reference>. <hi type="italic">He went into Galilee,</hi> for there he spent much of his time. Now see here, <div eID="gen26946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26947" type="x-p"/> 1. Whither Christ went; into Galilee, into the country of Galilee, but not to Nazareth, which was strictly <hi type="italic">his own</hi> country. He went among the villages, but declined going to Nazareth, the head city, for a reason here given, which <hi type="italic">Jesus himself testified,</hi> who knew the temper of his countrymen, the hearts of all men, and the experiences of all prophets, and it is this, That <hi type="italic">a prophet has no honour in his own country.</hi> Note, (1.) Prophets ought to have honour, because God has put honour upon them and we do or may receive benefit by them. (2.) The honour due to the Lord's prophets has very often been denied them, and contempt put upon them. (3.) This <hi type="italic">due</hi> honour is more frequently denied them <hi type="italic">in their own country;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Luke.4.24">Luke iv. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.57">Matt. xiii. 57</reference>. Not that it is universally true (no rule but has some exceptions), but it holds for the most part. Joseph, when he began to be a prophet, was most hated by his brethren; David was disdained by his brother (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.28">1 Sam. xvii. 28</reference>); Jeremiah was maligned by the men of Anathoth (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.21">Jer. xi. 21</reference>), Paul by his countrymen the Jews; and Christ's near kinsmen spoke most slightly of him, <reference osisRef="John.7.5">ch. vii. 5</reference>. Men's pride and envy make them scorn to be instructed by those who once were their school-fellows and play-fellows. Desire of novelty, and of that which is far-fetched and dear-bought, and seems to drop out of the sky to them, makes them despise those persons and things which they have been long used to and know the rise of. (4.) It is a great discouragement to a minister to go among a people who have no value for him or his labours. Christ would not go to Nazareth, because he knew how little respect he should have there. (5.) It is just with God to deny his gospel to those that despise the ministers of it. They that mock the messengers forfeit the benefit of the message. <reference osisRef="Matt.21.35">Matt. xxi. 35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.41">41</reference>. <div eID="gen26947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26948" type="x-p"/> 2. What entertainment he met with among the Galileans in the country (<reference osisRef="John.4.45">v. 45</reference>): They <hi type="italic">received him,</hi> bade him welcome, and cheerfully attended on his doctrine. Christ and his gospel are not sent in vain; if they have not honour with <hi type="italic">some,</hi> they shall have with <hi type="italic">others.</hi> Now the reason given why these Galileans were so ready to receive Christ is because they had seen <hi type="italic">the miracles he did at Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.45">v. 45</reference>. Observe, (1.) They went up to Jerusalem at the feast, the feast of the passover. The Galileans lay very remote from Jerusalem, and their way thither lay through the country of the Samaritans, which was troublesome for a Jew to pass through, worse than Baca's valley of old; yet, in obedience to God's command, they <hi type="italic">went up to the feast,</hi> and there they became acquainted with Christ. Note, They that are diligent and constant in attending on public ordinances some time or other meet with more spiritual benefit than they expect. (2.) At Jerusalem they <hi type="italic">saw</hi> Christ's miracles, which recommended him and his doctrine very much to their faith and affections. The miracles were wrought for the benefit of those at Jerusalem; yet the Galileans who were accidentally there got more advantage by them than they did for whom they were chiefly designed. Thus the word preached to a <hi type="italic">mixed multitude</hi> may perhaps edify <hi type="italic">occasional</hi> hearers more than the constant auditory. <div eID="gen26948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26949" type="x-p"/> 3. What city he went to. When he would go to a city, he chose to go to Cana of Galilee, <hi type="italic">where he had made the water wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.46">v. 46</reference>); thither he went, to see if there were any good fruits of that miracle remaining; and, if there were, to confirm their faith, and water what he had planted. The evangelist mentions this miracle here to teach us to keep in remembrance what we <hi type="italic">have seen</hi> of the works of Christ. <div eID="gen26949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26950" type="x-p"/> II. His <hi type="italic">curing</hi> the <hi type="italic">nobleman's son</hi> that was sick of a fever. This story is not recorded by any other of the evangelists; it comes in <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Matt. iv. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen26950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26951" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Who the <hi type="italic">petitioner</hi> was, and who the <hi type="italic">patient:</hi> the petitioner was a <hi type="italic">nobleman;</hi> the patient was his son: <hi type="italic">There was a certain nobleman. Regulus</hi> (so the Latin), a <hi type="italic">little king;</hi> so called, either for the largeness of his estate, or the extent of his power, or the royalties that belonged to his manor. Some understand it as denoting his <hi type="italic">preferment</hi>—he was a courtier in some office about the king; others as denoting his <hi type="italic">party</hi>—he was an Herodian, a royalist, a prerogative-man, one that espoused the interests of the Herods, father and son; perhaps it was Chuza, Herod's steward (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.3">Luke viii. 3</reference>), or Manæn, Herod's foster-brother, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1">Acts xiii. 1</reference>. There were saints in Cæsar's household. The father a nobleman, and yet the son sick; for dignities and titles of honour will be no security to persons and families from the assaults of sickness and death. It was fifteen miles from Capernaum where this nobleman lived to Cana, where Christ now was; yet this affliction in his family sent him so far to Christ. <div eID="gen26951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26952" type="x-p"/> 2. How the petitioner made <hi type="italic">his application</hi> to the physician. Having heard that <hi type="italic">Jesus was come out of</hi> Judea to Galilee, and finding that he did not come towards Capernaum, but turned off towards the other side of the country, he <hi type="italic">went to him</hi> himself, and <hi type="italic">besought him to come and heal his son,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.47">v. 47</reference>. See here, (1.) His <hi type="italic">tender affection</hi> to his son, that when he was sick he would spare no pains to get help for him. (2.) His <hi type="italic">great respect</hi> to our Lord Jesus, that he would come himself to wait upon him, when he might have sent a servant; and that he <hi type="italic">besought him,</hi> when, as a man in authority, some would think he might have ordered his attendance. The greatest men, when they come to God, must become beggars, and sue <hi type="italic">sub forma pauperis—as paupers.</hi> As to the errand he came upon, we may observe a mixture in <hi type="italic">his faith.</hi> [1.] There was <hi type="italic">sincerity</hi> in it; he did believe that Christ could heal his son, though his disease was dangerous. It is probable he had physicians to him, who had given him over; but he believed that Christ could cure him when the case seemed deplorable. [2.] Yet there was <hi type="italic">infirmity</hi> in his faith; he believed that Christ could heal his son, but, as it should seem, he thought he could not heal him at a distance, and therefore he besought him that he would <hi type="italic">come down</hi> and heal him, expecting, as Naaman did, that he would come and <hi type="italic">strike his hand</hi> over the patient, as if he could not cure him but by a <hi type="italic">physical contact.</hi> Thus we are apt to <hi type="italic">limit the Holy One of Israel,</hi> and to stint him to our forms. The centurion, a Gentile, a soldier, was so strong in faith as to say, <hi type="italic">Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.8">Matt. viii. 8</reference>. This nobleman, a Jew, must have Christ to come down, though it was a good day's journey, and despairs of a cure unless he come down, as if he must teach Christ how to work. We are encouraged to <hi type="italic">pray,</hi> but we are not allowed to prescribe: Lord, heal me; but, whether with a word or a touch, <hi type="italic">thy will be done.</hi> <div eID="gen26952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26953" type="x-p"/> 3. The gentle rebuke he met with in this address (<reference osisRef="John.4.48">v. 48</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jesus said to him,</hi> "I see how it is; <hi type="italic">except you see signs and wonders, you will not believe,</hi> as the Samaritans did, though they saw no signs and wonders, and therefore I must work miracles among you." Though he was a <hi type="italic">nobleman,</hi> and now in <hi type="italic">grief</hi> about his son, and had shown great respect to Christ in coming so far to him, yet Christ gives him a reproof. Men's dignity in the world shall not exempt them from the rebukes of the word or providence; for Christ reproves not <hi type="italic">after the hearing of his ears,</hi> but <hi type="italic">with equity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3-Isa.11.4">Isa. xi. 3, 4</reference>. Observe, Christ first shows him his sin and weakness, to prepare him for mercy, and then grants his request. Those whom Christ intends to honour with his <hi type="italic">favours</hi> he first <hi type="italic">humbles</hi> with his <hi type="italic">frowns.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Comforter</hi> shall first <hi type="italic">convince.</hi> Herod longed to see some miracle (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.8">Luke xxiii. 8</reference>), and this courtier was of the same mind, and the generality of the people too. Now that which is blamed is, (1.) That, whereas they had heard by credible and incontestable report of the miracles he had wrought in other places, they would not believe except they saw them with their own eyes, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.23">Luke iv. 23</reference>. They must be <hi type="italic">honoured,</hi> and they must be <hi type="italic">humoured,</hi> or they will not be <hi type="italic">convinced.</hi> Their country must be graced, and their curiosity gratified, with signs and wonders, or else, though the doctrine of Christ be sufficiently proved by miracles wrought elsewhere, they <hi type="italic">will not believe.</hi> Like Thomas, they will yield to no method of conviction but what they shall prescribe. (2.) That, whereas they had seen divers miracles, the evidence of which they could not gainsay, but which sufficiently proved Christ to be a teacher come from God, and should now have applied themselves to him for instruction in his doctrine, which by its native excellency would have <hi type="italic">gently led them on,</hi> in believing, to a spiritual perfection, instead of this they would go no further in believing than they were <hi type="italic">driven</hi> by signs and wonders. The <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> power of the word did not <hi type="italic">affect them,</hi> did not <hi type="italic">attract</hi> them, but only the <hi type="italic">sensible</hi> power of miracles, which were <hi type="italic">for those</hi> who believe not, while <hi type="italic">prophesying</hi> was for <hi type="italic">those that believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.22">1 Cor. xiv. 22</reference>. Those that admire <hi type="italic">miracles</hi> only, and <hi type="italic">despise prophesying,</hi> rank themselves with unbelievers. <div eID="gen26953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26954" type="x-p"/> 4. His continued importunity in his address (<reference osisRef="John.4.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sir, come down ere my child die.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kyrie</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Lord;</hi> so it should be rendered. In this reply of his we have, (1.) Something that was commendable: he took the reproof patiently; he spoke to Christ respectfully. Though he was one of those that wore soft clothing, yet he could bear reproof. It is none of the privileges of peerage to be above the reproofs of the word of Christ; but it is a sign of a good temper and disposition in men, especially in great men, when they can be told of their faults and not be angry. And, as he did not take the reproof for an affront, so he did not take it for a denial, but still prosecuted his request, and continued to wrestle till he prevailed. Nay, he might argue thus: "If Christ heal <hi type="italic">my soul,</hi> surely he will heal <hi type="italic">my son;</hi> if he cure <hi type="italic">my</hi> unbelief, he will cure <hi type="italic">his</hi> fever." This is the method Christ takes, first to work <hi type="italic">upon</hi> us, and then to work <hi type="italic">for</hi> us; and there is hope if we find him entering upon this method. (2.) Something that was blameworthy, that was his infirmity; for, [1.] He seems to take no notice of the reproof Christ gave him, says nothing to it, by way either of confession or of excuse, for he is so wholly taken up with concern about his child that he can mind nothing else. Note, The sorrow of the world is a great prejudice to our profiting by the word of Christ. Inordinate care and grief are thorns that choke the good seed; see <reference osisRef="Exod.6.9">Exod. vi. 9</reference>. [2.] He still discovered the weakness of his faith in the power of Christ. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He must have Christ to come down, thinking that else he could do the child no kindness. It is hard to persuade ourselves that distance of time and place are no obstructions to the knowledge and power of our Lord Jesus; yet so it is: he sees afar off, for his word, the word of his power, <hi type="italic">runs very swiftly. Secondly,</hi> He believes that Christ could heal a <hi type="italic">sick</hi> child, but not that he could raise a <hi type="italic">dead</hi> child, and therefore, "O <hi type="italic">come down, ere my child die,</hi>" as if then it would be too late; whereas Christ has the same power over death that he has over bodily diseases. He forgot that Elijah and Elisha had raised dead children; and is Christ's power inferior to theirs? Observe what haste he is in: <hi type="italic">Come down, ere my child die;</hi> as if there were danger of Christ's slipping his time. <hi type="italic">He that believeth does not make haste,</hi> but refers himself to Christ. "Lord, what and when and how thou pleasest." <div eID="gen26954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26955" type="x-p"/> 5. The answer of peace which Christ gave to his request at last (<reference osisRef="John.4.50">v. 50</reference>): <hi type="italic">Go thy way, thy son liveth.</hi> Christ here gives us an instance, (1.) Of his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> that he not only could heal, but could heal with so much ease, without the trouble of a visit. Here is nothing <hi type="italic">said,</hi> nothing <hi type="italic">done,</hi> nothing <hi type="italic">ordered</hi> to be done, and yet the cure wrought: <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth.</hi> The healing beams of the Sun of righteousness dispense benign influences from one end of heaven to another, and <hi type="italic">there is nothing hid from the heat thereof.</hi> Though Christ is now in heaven, and his church on earth, he can <hi type="italic">send from above.</hi> This nobleman would have Christ <hi type="italic">come down and heal his son;</hi> Christ will heal his son, and not <hi type="italic">come down.</hi> And thus the cure is the sooner wrought, the nobleman's mistake rectified, and his faith confirmed; so that the thing was better done in Christ's way. When he denies what we ask, he gives what is much more to our advantage; we ask for ease, he gives patience. Observe, His power was exerted by his word. In saying, <hi type="italic">Thy son lives,</hi> he showed that he has <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> and power to <hi type="italic">quicken whom he will.</hi> Christ's saying, <hi type="italic">Thy soul lives,</hi> makes it alive. (2.) Of his <hi type="italic">pity;</hi> he observed the nobleman to be <hi type="italic">in pain</hi> about his son, and his natural affection discovered itself in that word, <hi type="italic">Ere my child,</hi> my dear child, die; and therefore Christ dropped the reproof, and gave him assurance of the recovery of his child; for he knows how a father <hi type="italic">pities his children.</hi> <div eID="gen26955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26956" type="x-p"/> 6. The nobleman's belief of the word of Christ: He <hi type="italic">believed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">went away.</hi> Though Christ did not gratify him so far as to go down with him, he is satisfied with the method Christ took, and reckons he has gained his point. How quickly, how easily, is that which is lacking in our faith perfected by the word and power of Christ. Now he <hi type="italic">sees no sign or wonder,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">believes</hi> the wonder done. (1.) Christ said, <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth,</hi> and the man <hi type="italic">believed</hi> him; not only believed the omniscience of Christ, that he <hi type="italic">knew</hi> the child had recovered, but the omnipotence of Christ, that the cure was <hi type="italic">effected</hi> by his word. He left him <hi type="italic">dying;</hi> yet, when Christ said, <hi type="italic">He lives,</hi> like the father of the faithful, <hi type="italic">against hope he believed in hope,</hi> and <hi type="italic">staggered not through unbelief.</hi> (2.) Christ said, <hi type="italic">Go thy way;</hi> and, as an evidence of the sincerity of his faith, he <hi type="italic">went his way,</hi> and gave neither Christ nor himself any further disturbance. He did not press Christ to come down, did not say, "If he do recover, yet a visit will be acceptable;" no, he seems no further solicitous, but, like Hannah, he goes his way, and his countenance is <hi type="italic">no more sad.</hi> As one entirely satisfied, he made no great haste home; did not hurry home that night, but returned leisurely, as one that was perfectly easy in his own mind. <div eID="gen26956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26957" type="x-p"/> 7. The further confirmation of his faith, by comparing notes with his servants at his return. (1.) His servants met him with the agreeable news of the child's recovery, <reference osisRef="John.4.51">v. 51</reference>. Probably they met him not far from his own house, and, knowing what their master's cares were, they were willing as soon as they could to make him easy. David's servants were loth to tell him when the child was dead. Christ said, <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth;</hi> and now the servants say the same. Good news will meet those that hope in God's word. (2.) He enquired what hour the child began to recover (<reference osisRef="John.4.52">v. 52</reference>); not as if he doubted the influence of Christ's word upon the child's recovery, but he was desirous to have his faith confirmed, that he might be able to satisfy any to whom he should mention the miracle; for it was a material circumstance. Note, [1.] It is good to furnish ourselves with all the corroborating proofs and evidences that may be, to strengthen our faith in the word of Christ, that it may grow up to <hi type="italic">a full assurance. Show me a token for good.</hi> [2.] The diligent comparison of the works of Christ with his word will be of great use to us for the confirming of our faith. This was the course the nobleman took: <hi type="italic">He enquired of the servants the hour when he began to amend;</hi> and they told him, <hi type="italic">Yesterday at the seventh hour</hi> (at one o'clock in the afternoon, or, as some think this evangelist reckons, at seven o'clock at night) the <hi type="italic">fever left him;</hi> not only he began to amend, but he was perfectly well on a sudden; so <hi type="italic">the father knew that it was at the same hour</hi> when Jesus said to him, <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth.</hi> As the word of God, well-studied, will help us to understand his providences, so the providence of God, well observed, will help us to understand his word; for God is every day <hi type="italic">fulfilling the scripture.</hi> Two things would help to confirm his faith:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the child's recovery was <hi type="italic">sudden</hi> and not <hi type="italic">gradual.</hi> They name the precise time to an hour: <hi type="italic">Yesterday,</hi> not <hi type="italic">about,</hi> but <hi type="italic">at</hi> the seventh hour, <hi type="italic">the fever left him;</hi> not it <hi type="italic">abated,</hi> or began to <hi type="italic">decrease,</hi> but it <hi type="italic">left him</hi> in an instant. The word of Christ did not work like physic, which must have time to operate, and produce the effect, and perhaps <hi type="italic">cures by expectation</hi> only; no, with Christ it was <hi type="italic">dictum factum—he spoke and it was done;</hi> not, He spoke and it was <hi type="italic">set a doing. Secondly,</hi> That it was just at the same time that Christ spoke to him: <hi type="italic">at that very hour.</hi> The synchronisms and coincidents of events add very much to the beauty and harmony of Providence. Observe the <hi type="italic">time,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">thing</hi> itself will be more illustrious, for every thing is beautiful <hi type="italic">in its time;</hi> at the very time when it is <hi type="italic">promised,</hi> as Israel's deliverance (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exod. xii. 41</reference>); at the very time when it is <hi type="italic">prayed for,</hi> as Peter's deliverance, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Acts xii. 12</reference>. In men's works, distance of place is the delay of time and the retarding of business; but it is not so in the works of Christ. The pardon, and peace, and comfort, and spiritual healing, which he speaks in heaven, are, if he pleases, at the same time effected and wrought in the souls of believers; and, when these two come to be <hi type="italic">compared</hi> in the great day, Christ will be <hi type="italic">glorified in his saints, and admired in all them that believe.</hi> <div eID="gen26957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> 8. The <hi type="italic">happy effect and issue of this.</hi> The bringing of the cure to the family brought salvation to it. (1.) The nobleman <hi type="italic">himself believed.</hi> He had before <hi type="italic">believed</hi> the word of Christ, with reference to this particular occasion; but now he <hi type="italic">believed in Christ</hi> as the Messiah promised, and became one of his disciples. Thus the <hi type="italic">particular</hi> experience of the power and efficacy of <hi type="italic">one</hi> word of Christ may be a happy means to introduce and settle the whole authority of Christ's dominion in the soul. Christ has many ways of gaining the heart, and by the grant of a <hi type="italic">temporal</hi> mercy may make way for <hi type="italic">better</hi> things. (2.) His <hi type="italic">whole house</hi> believed likewise. [1.] Because of the <hi type="italic">interest</hi> they all had in the miracle, which preserved the <hi type="italic">blossom</hi> and <hi type="italic">hopes</hi> of the family; this affected them all, and endeared Christ to them, and recommended him to their best thoughts. [2.] Because of the <hi type="italic">influence</hi> the master of the family had upon them <hi type="italic">all.</hi> A master of a family cannot give faith to those under his charge, nor <hi type="italic">force</hi> them to believe, but he may be instrumental to remove <hi type="italic">external prejudices,</hi> which obstruct the operation of the evidence, and then the work is more than half done. <hi type="italic">Abraham</hi> was famous for this (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen. xviii. 19</reference>), and Joshua, <reference osisRef="John.24.15">ch. xxiv. 15</reference>. This was a <hi type="italic">nobleman,</hi> and probably he had a <hi type="italic">great household;</hi> but, when he comes into Christ's school, he brings them all along with him. What a blessed change was here in this house, occasioned by the sickness of the child! This should reconcile us to afflictions; we know not what good may follow from them. Probably, the conversion of this <hi type="italic">nobleman</hi> and his family at Capernaum might induce Christ to come afterwards, and settle at Capernaum, as his head-quarters in Galilee. When great men receive the gospel, they may be instrumental to bring it to the places where they live. <div eID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26959" type="x-p"/> 9. Here is the evangelist's remark upon this cure (<reference osisRef="John.4.54">v. 54</reference>); <hi type="italic">This is the second miracle,</hi> referring to <reference osisRef="John.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>, where the turning of water into wine is said to be the first; that was soon after his first return out of Judea, this soon after his second. In Judea he had wrought many miracles, <reference osisRef="John.3.2">ch. iii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.45">iv. 45</reference>. They had the first offer; but, being driven thence, he wrought miracles in Galilee. Somewhere or other Christ will find a welcome. People may, if they please, shut the sun out of <hi type="italic">their own houses,</hi> but they cannot shut it <hi type="italic">out of the world.</hi> This is noted to be the <hi type="italic">second</hi> miracle, 1. To remind us of the first, wrought in the same place some months before. <hi type="italic">Fresh</hi> mercies should revive the remembrance of former mercies, as former mercies should encourage our hopes of further mercies. Christ keeps account of his favours, whether we do or no. 2. To let us know that <hi type="italic">this</hi> cure was <hi type="italic">before</hi> those many cures which the other evangelists mention to be wrought in Galilee, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Matt. iv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.1.34">Mark i. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.40">Luke iv. 40</reference>. Probably, the patient being a person of quality, the cure was the more talked of and sent him crowds of patients; when this nobleman applied himself to Christ, multitudes followed. What abundance of good may great men do, if they be good men!  <chapter eID="John.4"/> <div eID="gen26959" type="x-p"/>

entries.0ec41eb42020b9be627d7046971ad4f45c89dd22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14922"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.4.1-John.4.42">Joh 4:1-42</reference>. Christ and the Woman of Samaria--The Samaritans of Sychar.</title> <div sID="gen28792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14922"/><hi type="bold">1-4. the Lord knew--</hi>not by report, but in the sense of <reference osisRef="John.2.25">Joh 2:25</reference>, for which reason He is here styled "the Lord." <div eID="gen28792" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5590fc64755e82c69bb358d92c69fdf4482f54e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14926"/><div sID="gen28797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14926"/><hi type="bold">5. cometh ... to--</hi>that is, as far as: for He remained at some distance from it.<div eID="gen28797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sychar--</hi>the "Shechem" of the Old Testament, about thirty-four miles from Jerusalem, afterwards called "Neapolis," and now "Nablous." <div eID="gen28798" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fc521c16f7c86d2a695bbec45d23e6793a7228b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14927"/><div sID="gen28799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14927"/><hi type="bold">6-8. wearied ... sat thus--</hi>that is, "as you might fancy a weary man would"; an instance of the graphic style of St. John [Webster and Wilkinson]. In fact, this is perhaps the most human of all the scenes of our Lord's earthly history. We seem to be beside Him, overhearing all that is here recorded, nor could any painting of the scene on canvas, however perfect, do other than lower the conception which this exquisite narrative conveys to the devout and intelligent reader. But with all that is human, how much also of the divine have we here, both blended in one glorious manifestation of the majesty, grace, pity, patience with which "the Lord" imparts light and life to this unlikeliest of strangers, standing midway between Jews and heathens.<div eID="gen28799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sixth hour--</hi>noonday, reckoning from six A.M. From <reference osisRef="Song.1.7">So 1:7</reference> we know, as from other sources, that the very flocks "rested at noon." But Jesus, whose maxim was, "I must work the works of Him that sent Me while it is day" (<reference osisRef="John.9.4">Joh 9:4</reference>), seems to have denied Himself that repose, at least on this occasion, probably that He might reach this well when He knew the woman would be there. Once there, however, He accepts ... the grateful ease of a seat on the patriarchal stone. But what music is that which I hear from His lips, "Come unto Me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Mt 11:28</reference>). <div eID="gen28800" type="x-p"/>
entries.23cabcb46e542534187830497191c2c8e62c168f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14929"/><div sID="gen28802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14929"/><hi type="bold">9-12.
